title: IGA-ODIL: Optimizing DIscretre robust Loss with Isogeometric Analysis to solve forward and inverse problems faster using machine learning tools
authors: Maciej Paszyński, Tomasz Służalec
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) formulate the solution of partial differential equations as residual minimization problems over neural network parameterizations. Although highly flexible, optimization of PINNs using modern variants of Stochastic Gradient Descent algorithms is expensive. On the other hand, iterative computation of PINN parameterization using the Gauss-Newton method suffers from convergence difficulties, dense Jacobian structures, and poor conditioning that limit the effectiveness of second-order optimization methods. In this work, we introduce IGA-ODIL, a spline-based residual minimization framework combining ideas from Optimizing DIscrete Loss (ODIL), robust variational residual minimization, and Isogeometric Analysis (IGA). Instead of neural-network parameterizations of PINNs, the unknown solution is represented by smooth B-spline basis functions, leading to sparse structured Jacobians and efficient Gauss--Newton optimization. We also derive robust residual formulations based on weighted Gram operators, making the loss function related with the true error. The resulting systems inherit locality, sparsity, and approximation-theoretic properties of classical finite element and isogeometric methods while preserving the residual-learning philosophy of scientific machine learning. The proposed methodology is evaluated on several benchmark problems, including Poisson equations, convection-dominated advection--diffusion equations, Helmholtz problems with highly oscillatory solutions, nonlinear Allen--Cahn equations, and inverse Helmholtz parameter identification. Numerical experiments demonstrate orders-of-magnitude speedups compared with PINNs and CRVPINNs while maintaining high accuracy and robustness.

infographic.key_insight: IGA-ODIL replaces neural-network parameterization with smooth B-spline bases and robust residual minimization, enabling much faster and better-conditioned PDE solving than standard PINNs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes forward and inverse simulation for difficult PDEs more practical in engineering workflows by improving speed, sparsity, and solver robustness.
method: Represent unknown fields with B-spline / isogeometric basis functions instead of neural nets
Minimize a robust discrete residual using weighted Gram-operator loss
Solve the resulting sparse system efficiently with Gauss-Newton optimization
infographic.evidence_signal: The method was benchmarked on Poisson, advection-diffusion, Helmholtz, Allen-Cahn, and inverse Helmholtz problems, with reported orders-of-magnitude speedups over PINNs and CRVPINNs while preserving high accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on spline-space setup and Gauss-Newton convergence, so implementation details and problem conditioning may still affect robustness.
infographic.paper_title: IGA-ODIL: Optimizing DIscretre robust Loss with Isogeometric Analysis to solve forward and inverse problems faster using machine learning tools

title: SoundnessBench: Can Your AI Scientist Really Tell Good Research Ideas from Bad Ones?
authors: Sy-Tuyen Ho, Minghui Liu, Huy Nghiem, Furong Huang
abstract: Autonomous AI research agents aim to accelerate scientific discovery by automating the research pipeline, from hypothesis generation to peer review. However, existing benchmarks rarely test a fundamental bottleneck: whether Large Language Models can judge the methodological viability of a research idea before expending time and computational resources. We introduce SoundnessBench, a curated benchmark of 1,099 machine-learning research proposals reconstructed from ICLR submissions, labeled with reviewer soundness sub-scores, and audited against source papers. SoundnessBench should be interpreted as a benchmark for recoverable proposal-stage soundness rather than exact prediction of full-paper review outcomes. Across 12 frontier LLMs, we find a pervasive optimism bias: under standard prompting, models frequently rate low-soundness proposals as sound, while aggressive prompting largely shifts errors from false positives to false negatives. Additional controls for public-corpus contamination, paper-identifying phrases, surface features, and human audit quality suggest that this behavior is not explained by a single confounder. Our results indicate that current LLMs are not yet reliable as standalone first-gate evaluators for scientific rigor.

infographic.key_insight: SoundnessBench shows that frontier LLMs often overrate weak research ideas, revealing an optimism bias that makes them unreliable as first-pass judges of methodological soundness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For AI-assisted research workflows, this means LLMs should be used as aids to screening and critique, not as standalone gatekeepers for deciding which ideas deserve compute and development time.
method: Built SoundnessBench from 1,099 ML research proposals reconstructed from ICLR submissions.
Annotated proposals with reviewer soundness sub-scores and audited them against source papers.
Evaluated 12 frontier LLMs under standard and aggressive prompting, plus controls for contamination and surface cues.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark uses 1,099 reconstructed proposals with reviewer soundness labels, and the evaluation across 12 frontier LLMs found systematic false positives under standard prompting.
infographic.watch_item: SoundnessBench targets recoverable proposal-stage soundness, so it should not be treated as a direct predictor of full-paper review outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: SoundnessBench: Can Your AI Scientist Really Tell Good Research Ideas from Bad Ones?

title: Meta-Cognitive Memory Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
authors: Ziyan Liu, Zhezheng Hao, Yeqiu Chen, Hong Wang, Jingren Hou, Ruiyi Ding
abstract: Memory-augmented LLM agents tackle complex long-horizon tasks by recursively summarizing interaction trajectories into compact memory. However, existing approaches typically train these memory policies using outcome-based reinforcement learning, failing to localize where intermediate memory quality degrades. As interactions unfold, ambiguous recursive summaries progressively discard task-relevant information and introduce semantic noise. This exacerbates belief deviation, obscuring the agent's estimate of the latent task state and ultimately derailing long-horizon reasoning. We therefore argue that memory optimization should focus not merely on trajectory-level success, but on the clarity of the belief induced by intermediate summaries. To this end, we introduce Belief Entropy, a self-supervised proxy that probes how uncertain the model remains about the latent task state given its current memory. Based on this proxy, we propose Metacognitive Memory Policy Optimization (MMPO). Instead of relying only on sparse outcome-based signals, MMPO provides fine-grained, memory-specific supervision via explicitly penalizing summaries that induce high epistemic uncertainty. Experiments show that MMPO consistently outperforms existing methods on diverse long-horizon tasks, maintaining 97.1% performance even when scaled to 1.75M-token contexts.

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that long-horizon LLM agents fail when recursive memory summaries become ambiguous, and proposes optimizing memory quality by minimizing the uncertainty those summaries induce about the latent task state.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For building reliable agents, this suggests memory policies should be trained with fine-grained uncertainty-aware feedback, not just sparse task success signals.
method: Define Belief Entropy as a self-supervised proxy for uncertainty about the latent task state given current memory.
Use Metacognitive Memory Policy Optimization (MMPO) to penalize summaries that create high epistemic uncertainty.
Provide memory-specific supervision to reduce semantic noise and belief deviation during recursive summarization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that MMPO outperforms prior methods on diverse long-horizon tasks and retains 97.1% performance even at 1.75M-token context length.
infographic.watch_item: Belief-entropy estimates may be sensitive to proxy quality and implementation details, so the method’s robustness depends on how well uncertainty is calibrated.
infographic.paper_title: Meta-Cognitive Memory Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents

title: SchGen: PCB Schematic Generation with Semantic-Grounded Code Representations
authors: Qinpei Luo, Ruichun Ma, Xinyu Zhang, Lili Qiu
abstract: Printed circuit board (PCB) schematic design defines nearly all electronic hardware, but it remains manual and expertise-intensive. While generative AI has advanced digital and analog IC design, PCB schematic generation from natural-language intent is largely unexplored. This paper presents SchGen, the first large language model that generates editable PCB schematics from natural-language requests. The key challenge lies in the lack of an LLM-suited representation and a large-scale dataset. Current schematic formats are dominated by verbose, tool-specific syntax and geometry-heavy descriptions, making them difficult to generate reliably. We introduce a semantically grounded code representation that encodes schematic editing primitives with relative placement and pin-name-based wiring, transforming a geometry-driven generation problem into a semantics-driven matching task amenable to LLMs. We further construct a large-scale dataset of PCB schematics paired with user prompts via a human-agent collaborative pipeline that converts open-source hardware designs into our representation. Experiments show that SchGen significantly outperforms alternative representations and even larger general-purpose LLMs on wire connectivity accuracy and functional correctness. Our results highlight the critical role of representation design in enabling generative models for complex hardware design tasks.

infographic.key_insight: SchGen shows that PCB schematics can be generated by LLMs when the design is recast into a semantically grounded code representation instead of geometry-heavy tool syntax.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This could make PCB schematic drafting faster and more accessible by turning natural-language hardware intent into editable, connectivity-correct schematics.
method: Defines schematic editing primitives with relative placement and pin-name-based wiring.
Converts generation from geometry-driven drawing to semantics-driven matching for LLMs.
Builds a large-scale prompt-schematic dataset from open-source hardware via a human-agent collaborative pipeline.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that SchGen outperforms alternative representations and larger general-purpose LLMs on wire connectivity accuracy and functional correctness.
infographic.watch_item: Performance likely depends on the quality of the new representation and dataset coverage, so unusual component topologies or tool-specific constraints may still be challenging.
infographic.paper_title: SchGen: PCB Schematic Generation with Semantic-Grounded Code Representations

title: ProjectionBench: Evaluating Scientific Hypothesis Generation in LLMs Under Progressive Information Disclosure
authors: A. J. Lew, Y. Cao, M. J. Buehler
abstract: Scientific discovery is an inherently creative and uncertain process, requiring reasoning beyond the recall of known knowledge. While many benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate large language model (LLM) performance on deep research tasks via multi-hop retrieval, their innovative reasoning abilities essential for true scientific discovery remain largely untested. We introduce a benchmark framework for evaluating model performance in scientific discovery and reasoning, building up from a raw problem to the classical null hypothesis test. In our framework, models initially receive only the topic and research question from a recent paper, with technical details progressively revealed. At each stage of information disclosure, the model is tasked with generating hypotheses that address the research question, which is compared with the conclusions from the original paper and evaluated via automated semantic similarity of constituent atomic claims. This progressive evaluation of semantic divergence from ground-truth conclusions enables assessment of a model's innovativeness (under minimal information) to grounded reasoning capabilities (under full experimental details), both critical for using LLMs for scientific discovery purposes. Our framework provides a foundation for systematically evaluating scientific reasoning and discovery capabilities in LLMs, crucial for advancing the development of next-generation AI scientist/co-scientist systems. Specifically, here we evaluate GPT-5, GPT-5.4, Gemini 2.5 pro, and Gemini 3.1 pro preview across 45 papers spanning bioactive materials, mechanical materials, and nanomaterials. We find that GPT-5.4 and Gemini 3.1 pro outperform their previous generation counterparts as expected, and GPT-5.4 in particular maintains 0.7 F1 score alignment with ground truth conclusions even under minimal context.

infographic.key_insight: ProjectionBench measures how well LLMs generate scientific hypotheses as progressively more experimental information is revealed, separating novelty under sparse context from grounded reasoning under full context.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The benchmark offers a practical way to compare and improve AI scientist systems for materials and other discovery workflows, especially when models must reason from incomplete problem statements.
method: Start with only a paper’s topic and research question.
Reveal details stepwise up to the classical null-hypothesis test.
Score model hypotheses against paper conclusions using semantic similarity over atomic claims.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors evaluated GPT-5, GPT-5.4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview on 45 papers across bioactive materials, mechanical materials, and nanomaterials, and report GPT-5.4 reached about 0.7 F1 alignment with ground-truth conclusions even under minimal context.
infographic.watch_item: Semantic-similarity scoring may miss scientifically valid but differently framed hypotheses, so the benchmark should be used with care when comparing models that express conclusions in diverse ways.
infographic.paper_title: ProjectionBench: Evaluating Scientific Hypothesis Generation in LLMs Under Progressive Information Disclosure

title: Unifying Temporal and Structural Credit Assignment in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Prompt Optimization
authors: Wenwu Li, Yuran Song, Mingze Zhao, Bo Jin, Wenhao Li
abstract: While Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) empower Large Language Models to tackle complex reasoning tasks through collaborative interaction, optimizing their dynamics remains a formidable challenge due to the discrete, non-differentiable nature of the computation graph and the sparsity of global supervisory signals. Existing black-box optimizers struggle to attribute trajectory-level failure to specific local components, resulting in inefficient, high-variance exploration. We argue that tractable MAS optimization needs structural inductive biases to disentangle error signals. We propose temporal and structural credit assignment, which decomposes the objective along two axes: (i) temporal credit, using state-space bottlenecks to identify critical rounds, and (ii) structural credit, using stationary role policies to isolate agent contributions. Leveraging these decomposed signals, we introduce a discrete, verbalized block coordinate descent algorithm for iterative refinement. Rather than indiscriminate global updates, it alternates between optimizing role prompts and aggregation protocols, using LLM-generated "proxy gradients" to target only the identified weak links. Across diverse reasoning benchmarks, our approach substantially reduces query complexity while improving performance, providing a principled and interpretable path toward self-improving MAS.

infographic.key_insight: The paper decomposes multi-agent prompt optimization into temporal and structural credit assignment so LLM systems can pinpoint which rounds and which agents are causing failures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a more sample-efficient, interpretable way to tune multi-agent LLM workflows by updating only the weakest links instead of doing broad black-box search.
method: Temporal credit: use state-space bottlenecks to identify critical rounds in the interaction trajectory.
Structural credit: use stationary role policies to isolate each agent’s contribution to the outcome.
Optimization: alternate verbalized block coordinate descent over role prompts and aggregation protocols with LLM-generated proxy gradients.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation across diverse reasoning benchmarks, showing lower query complexity while improving performance.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on reliable proxy gradients and decomposed credit signals, which may be sensitive to prompt design and harder to stabilize in complex MAS settings.
infographic.paper_title: Unifying Temporal and Structural Credit Assignment in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Prompt Optimization

title: CalArena: A Large-Scale Post-Hoc Calibration Benchmark
authors: Eugène Berta, David Holzmüller, Francis Bach, Michael I. Jordan
abstract: Reliable probability estimates are critical in many machine learning applications, yet modern classifiers are often poorly calibrated. Post-hoc calibration provides a simple and widely used solution, but the large number of proposed methods, combined with small-scale and inconsistent evaluations, makes it difficult to determine which approaches are truly effective in practice. We introduce a large-scale, standardized benchmark for post-hoc calibration, covering nearly 2000 experiments across tabular and computer vision tasks, including binary, multiclass, and large-scale classification settings. Our benchmark aggregates predictions from a diverse set of classical models, modern deep learning architectures, and foundation models, and provides unified, reproducible implementations of dozens of calibration methods within a common evaluation framework. We argue that Post-Hoc Improvement (PHI) in proper scoring rules offers a principled alternative to traditional calibration error estimators for comparing post-hoc methods, capturing both calibration quality and potential degradation to the model's predictive performance. Using this framework, we conduct the most comprehensive empirical study of post-hoc calibration to date. Our results reveal consistent patterns across domains: smooth calibration functions outperform binning-based approaches, dedicated multiclass methods are essential in high-dimensional settings, and generic machine learning models are not competitive without calibration-specific design. To facilitate future research, we release all data, code, and evaluation tools, providing a plug-and-play benchmark for developing and comparing calibration methods.

infographic.key_insight: CalArena shows that post-hoc calibration methods need standardized, large-scale evaluation, and that smooth, calibration-specific approaches consistently outperform simple binning-based methods.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For deployed ML systems that rely on trustworthy probabilities, the benchmark helps practitioners choose calibration methods that improve reliability without undermining predictive performance.
method: Aggregated nearly 2000 experiments across tabular and vision tasks, spanning binary, multiclass, and large-scale classification.
Benchmarked predictions from classical models, deep networks, and foundation models using a common reproducible framework.
Compared dozens of post-hoc calibration methods with Post-Hoc Improvement (PHI) in proper scoring rules as the primary evaluation criterion.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study compiles a large, standardized benchmark with nearly 2000 experiments and unified implementations across diverse datasets, models, and calibration settings.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend on the quality of the underlying predictions and on careful multiclass handling, so generic calibration methods may fail in high-dimensional settings.
infographic.paper_title: CalArena: A Large-Scale Post-Hoc Calibration Benchmark

title: Statistical Embeddings for Similarity, Retrieval, and Interpretable Alignment of Numeric Tabular Datasets
authors: M. Ross Kunz, John Merickel, Keith Wilson
abstract: Numeric tabular datasets are the dominant data format in scientific practice, yet large language models lack native mechanisms for representing numeric datasets in a meaningful way across heterogeneous feature spaces. Existing approaches either target predictive modeling over individual datasets, which requires a shared set of variable definitions, or lack mechanisms for interpretable cross-dataset alignment. The proposed methodology characterizes numeric tabular datasets through structured exploratory data analysis descriptors, embeds those descriptors into a shared vector space using a pretrained sentence transformer, and quantifies cross-dataset similarity via Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA). Furthermore, a penalized formulation of CCA is applied to recover sparse, interpretable variable-level correspondences between datasets, identifying which statistical descriptors or variable-level quantities drive cross-dataset alignment without requiring shared variable names or feature conventions. Differential privacy is optionally applied to the descriptor set prior to embedding, supporting deployment in sensitive data contexts without requiring access to raw observations at time of comparison. The methodology is evaluated across 15 datasets spanning general-purpose benchmarks, materials informatics, and nuclear-grade graphite characterization. Results demonstrate a total P@1 score of 0.9, with known nearest-neighbor retrieval and cluster structure remaining robust across embedding ablations and differential privacy budgets. The proposed framework provides a principled pathway for integrating heterogeneous numeric data into retrieval-augmented generation pipelines while preserving statistical context, with direct applications to data-driven algorithm selection and simulation model initialization for unknown datasets.

infographic.key_insight: The paper turns numeric tabular datasets into comparable statistical embeddings, enabling retrieval and interpretable cross-dataset alignment even when feature names and conventions differ.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical way to match unknown datasets to prior examples for data-driven model selection, simulation initialization, and retrieval-augmented workflows.
method: Compute structured exploratory-data-analysis descriptors for each dataset.
Embed descriptors into a shared vector space with a pretrained sentence transformer, then measure similarity with CCA.
Use penalized CCA to recover sparse, interpretable variable-level correspondences; optionally add differential privacy before embedding.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 15 datasets, the method achieved a total P@1 of 0.9, with nearest-neighbor retrieval and clustering remaining robust under embedding ablations and differential privacy budgets.
infographic.watch_item: Descriptor quality, CCA sparsity settings, and privacy budget choices may materially affect alignment stability and interpretability on new datasets.
infographic.paper_title: Statistical Embeddings for Similarity, Retrieval, and Interpretable Alignment of Numeric Tabular Datasets

title: LLUMI: Improving LLM Writing Assistance for Mental Health Support with Online Community Feedback
authors: Jiwon Kim, Maya Ajit, Sherry Gong, Soorya Ram Shimgekar, Dong Whi Yoo, Eshwar Chandrasekharan
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promise in generating supportive responses for mental health queries, but improving their usefulness, empathy, and safety often requires substantial compute, expert input, and labeled data. At the same time, deploying proprietary, cloud-based models for mental health-related interactions raises important privacy and data-governance concerns, given the sensitivities. To address this challenge, we introduce LLUMI setup that can be hosted in-house within protected environments. LLUMI consists of two complementary components: a generation model (GM), which drafts supportive responses to mental health queries, and an improvement model (IM), which revises an initial human-crafted response. We leverage feedback signals from Reddit mental health communities, using community endorsement patterns such as upvotes and downvotes to construct chosen-rejected response pairs for Supervised Fine Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). We further align LLUMI using human evaluation across five dimensions: readability, empathy, connection, actionability, and safety. Our results show that, despite relying on smaller open-source models rather than proprietary cloud-based GPT models, LLUMI achieves comparable performance across linguistic analyses and human evaluations. These findings suggest that open-source models, when trained with community-derived preference signals, can support high-quality mental health support assistance while offering a more privacy-preserving alternative for sensitive support contexts.

infographic.key_insight: LLUMI shows that smaller open-source LLMs can be improved for mental-health support by learning from community preference signals and human safety-focused feedback.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work offers a privacy-preserving, in-house alternative to proprietary cloud models for deploying mental-health writing assistance in protected environments.
method: Build a two-part system: a generation model (GM) for drafting supportive replies and an improvement model (IM) for revising human-written responses.
Use Reddit mental-health community feedback (upvotes/downvotes) to form chosen-rejected pairs for SFT and DPO.
Align outputs with human ratings on readability, empathy, connection, actionability, and safety.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that LLUMI achieves comparable performance to proprietary GPT-based models in linguistic analyses and human evaluations using community-derived preference data.
infographic.watch_item: Community votes are an imperfect proxy for clinical quality, so deployment still needs careful safety review and domain oversight.
infographic.paper_title: LLUMI: Improving LLM Writing Assistance for Mental Health Support with Online Community Feedback

title: HPO: Hysteretic Policy Optimization for Stable and Efficient Training under Sparse-Reward Regime
authors: Mohamed Sana, Nicola Piovesan, Antonio De Domenico, Fadhel Ayed, Haozhe Zhang
abstract: We investigate a narrow but common failure mode of GRPO-style reinforcement learning in the context of sparse verifiable rewards: early updates contain more responses with negative advantages than those with positive advantages, while response-level length normalization ties the magnitude of the update to the length of the output. We propose Hysteretic Policy Optimization (HPO), a minimal modification of GRPO that reduces the weight of negative-advantage updates and replaces per-response length normalization with mean-length normalization. We further introduce Adaptive HPO (A-HPO), which sets the hysteretic weight based on batch-level advantage-sign statistics, thereby removing the need for tuning a fixed hysteretic weight. In our TeleLogs and Countdown experiments, A-HPO improves the reward per update compared to GRPO, with the largest gains in early sparse reward regimes. On TeleLogs, A-HPO achieves a final reward of 0.84, outperforming SAPO by 5%, GSPO by 11%, and GRPO by 15%, while maintaining a comparable response-length. On Countdown, A-HPO achieves the largest gains in initial and most difficult configurations across 1.5B-7B models. Ablation studies on the hysteretic weight show that the gains of A-HPO come from better balancing the contributions of positive and negative advantages compared to positive-only or fully symmetric updates.

infographic.key_insight: Hysteretic Policy Optimization (HPO) stabilizes sparse-reward RL by down-weighting negative-advantage updates and using mean-length normalization, with Adaptive HPO (A-HPO) automatically setting that balance from batch statistics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a simple drop-in change to GRPO-style training that can improve sample efficiency and early-stage learning when rewards are sparse and verifiable.
method: Reduce the update weight for negative-advantage responses instead of treating all advantages symmetrically.
Replace per-response length normalization with mean-length normalization to decouple update magnitude from output length.
Use A-HPO to adapt the hysteretic weight from batch-level advantage-sign statistics, removing manual tuning.
infographic.evidence_signal: In TeleLogs and Countdown experiments, A-HPO improved reward per update over GRPO, with the biggest gains in early sparse-reward regimes and a final TeleLogs reward of 0.84.
infographic.watch_item: The adaptive hysteretic rule may depend on reliable batch advantage-sign statistics, so behavior could vary with batch size, reward sparsity, and task-specific reward noise.
infographic.paper_title: HPO: Hysteretic Policy Optimization for Stable and Efficient Training under Sparse-Reward Regime

title: RL2ML: Finite-Rollout Surrogate Objectives from Reinforcement Learning to Maximum Likelihood
authors: Yifu Zheng
abstract: Correctness-based Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) trains language models from binary feedback on sampled outputs, but the objective optimized in expectation and the stochastic update geometry induced by finite rollout groups are often conflated. This paper develops RL2ML, a family of finite-rollout surrogate objectives with a closed-form, exactly unbiased gradient estimator. The family continuously connects standard reinforcement learning, maximum-likelihood-like training, and beyond-maximum-likelihood objectives while preserving estimator-objective alignment under a fixed rollout budget. We introduce the group-level update scale to characterize how a rollout group is reweighted after its empirical success count is observed, revealing a subcritical-supercritical update-scale transition that is hidden by population-level objective notation alone. Building on this distinction, calibrated metric-gain analysis and exact variance decomposition show that the best choice of surrogate objective is determined neither by proximity to maximum likelihood nor by the population-level weight alone. Instead, it depends jointly on the evaluation metric, local sensitivity, and estimator variance. The remaining degree of freedom in the surrogate objective family can therefore be formulated as a one-dimensional optimization problem rather than treated as an unconstrained hyperparameter.

infographic.key_insight: RL2ML shows that finite-rollout training can be reframed as a family of surrogate objectives that exactly match the gradient of the sampled update, bridging reinforcement learning and maximum-likelihood-style training without objective-gradient mismatch.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For practical LLM training with limited rollout budgets, the framework helps choose update rules based on metric sensitivity and variance, not just on whether the objective looks more like RL or MLE.
method: Defines a continuum of finite-rollout surrogate objectives spanning RL, MLE-like, and beyond-MLE behavior.
Derives a closed-form, exactly unbiased gradient estimator aligned with the sampled rollout update.
Introduces group-level update scale and uses metric-gain plus variance analysis to reduce objective choice to a 1D optimization problem.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports calibrated metric-gain analysis and exact variance decomposition, showing the best surrogate depends jointly on evaluation metric, local sensitivity, and estimator variance.
infographic.watch_item: The framework is theoretically elegant, but selecting the optimal surrogate still requires reliable estimates of local metric sensitivity and variance, which may be noisy or task-dependent in practice.
infographic.paper_title: RL2ML: Finite-Rollout Surrogate Objectives from Reinforcement Learning to Maximum Likelihood

title: Efficient Test-Time Finetuning of LLMs via Convex Reconstruction and Gradient Caching
authors: Alaa Khamis, Alaa Maalouf
abstract: Test-time finetuning (TTFT) is a rapidly evolving paradigm that adapts a language model to each prompt by retrieving related sequences, updating the model on them, and then evaluating the prompt. However, TTFT is only practical if it is fast: selection and finetuning both happen per query, making each a direct bottleneck. Existing methods trade speed for quality: fast retrieval is often redundant, while stronger diversity-aware selection adds prohibitive per-query cost. We introduce HullFT, a geometric approach to TTFT that addresses both bottlenecks. Given a query, HullFT first represents the query embedding as a sparse convex combination of few training sequences, using efficient projection-free Frank-Wolfe optimization. This yields a support set that is inherently relevant and diverse. We then convert the fractional convex weights into an exact integer multiset for finetuning through a geometric integerization procedure. The resulting multiplicities naturally create repeated examples, which we exploit with Gradient Reuse to amortize forward-backward computation across repeated finetuning steps. Our experiments show that HullFT improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff over current state-of-the-art TTFT methods, achieving lower bits-per-byte at substantially lower total runtime.

infographic.key_insight: HullFT makes test-time finetuning faster and better by selecting a sparse, diverse support set with convex geometry, then reusing gradients across repeated examples.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method targets a practical deployment bottleneck in per-query LLM adaptation, improving the quality–runtime tradeoff for retrieval-and-finetune pipelines.
method: Use Frank-Wolfe to approximate the query as a sparse convex combination of training sequence embeddings.
Integerize the fractional weights into a multiset for finetuning, creating repeated examples.
Apply Gradient Reuse to amortize forward-backward cost across those repetitions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports lower bits-per-byte at substantially lower total runtime than current state-of-the-art TTFT methods.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on efficient nearest-neighbor retrieval, stable convex optimization, and correct handling of repeated-example gradient caching at inference time.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Test-Time Finetuning of LLMs via Convex Reconstruction and Gradient Caching

title: How LoRA Remembers? A Parametric Memory Law for LLM Finetuning
authors: Ziwen Xu, Haiwen Hong, Linsong Yu, Benglei Cui, Longtao Huang, Hui Xue
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) must continuously learn and update knowledge to remain effective in dynamic real-world environments. While Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is widely used for such memory updates, existing studies mainly rely on qualitative downstream evaluations, leaving the quantitative capacity limits and underlying dynamics of exact parametric memory largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we employ LoRA as a controlled memory capacity probe within the latent space to systematically quantify exact parametric memory. We introduce the Parametric Memory Law, a robust power law linking loss reduction Delta L to effective parameters and sequence length. At the token level, fine-grained analysis reveals a deterministic phase transition, demonstrating that a prediction probability of p > 0.5 constitutes a sufficient condition for verbatim recall under greedy decoding. Driven by these insights, we introduce MemFT, a threshold-guided optimization strategy that dynamically redistributes the training budget toward sub-threshold tokens. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that MemFT can enhance memory fidelity and efficiency. Code will be released at https://github.com/zjunlp/ParametricMemoryLaw.

infographic.key_insight: LoRA can be treated as a controllable probe for exact parametric memory, and the paper identifies a robust power-law relationship between memory gain, effective parameters, and sequence length.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results provide a quantitative rule for allocating fine-tuning budget more efficiently when updating LLM knowledge, especially under tight compute or memory constraints.
method: Use LoRA as a controlled memory-capacity probe in latent space.
Fit a Parametric Memory Law linking loss reduction (ΔL) to effective parameters and sequence length.
Design MemFT to shift training toward sub-threshold tokens using a prediction-probability threshold.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports systematic quantitative analysis at both sequence and token levels, including a deterministic phase transition and empirical evaluation showing improved memory fidelity and efficiency with MemFT.
infographic.watch_item: The p > 0.5 greedy-decoding threshold and the observed law may depend on model, data, and finetuning setup, so transferability should be validated before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: How LoRA Remembers? A Parametric Memory Law for LLM Finetuning

title: In-Context Reward Adaptation for Robust Preference Modeling
authors: Zhenyu Sun, Zheng Xu, Ermin Wei
abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) typically relies on static reward models to align Large Language Models with human preferences. However, human values are inherently diverse and heterogeneous, and a single reward model often lacks the robustness required to generalize to unseen preference domains. While existing multi-reward frameworks attempt to address this, they are often restricted to a fixed set of known domains and fail to adapt to unseen human distributions without costly retraining. In this work, we propose In-Context Reward Adaptation, a transformer-based framework designed to model diverse and unseen human preferences on the fly. By leveraging the in-context learning capabilities of transformers, our approach adaptively infers the underlying reward structure from a small set of preference demonstrations. We demonstrate that while a standard transformer architecture is insufficient for this task by characterizing an asymptotic bias to the ground-truth, incorporating human response time as an auxiliary input signal enables the model to successfully adapt to preferences from previously unseen domains. Our findings show that this approach provides a more robust foundation for preference modeling, allowing for the representation of heterogeneous rewards and preference distribution shift, and offering a scalable path toward more flexible human-AI alignment.

infographic.key_insight: A transformer can infer reward preferences from a few demonstrations, but robust adaptation to unseen human preference domains requires an added signal such as response time.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more flexible RLHF systems that can generalize across heterogeneous user values without retraining a separate reward model for every new domain.
method: Use in-context preference demonstrations to infer latent reward structure on the fly.
Augment the transformer input with human response time as an auxiliary signal.
Compare standard transformer behavior against the adapted model to assess unseen-domain generalization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports characterizing an asymptotic bias in a standard transformer and showing that adding response time enables successful adaptation to previously unseen preference domains.
infographic.watch_item: Response time must be reliably measured and may introduce sensitivity to noisy or context-dependent human interaction signals.
infographic.paper_title: In-Context Reward Adaptation for Robust Preference Modeling

title: Mean-Field Diffuser: Scaling Offline MARL to Thousands of Agents
authors: Wenhao Li, Xiangfeng Wang, Bo Jin
abstract: Diffusion-based planning has achieved strong results in single-agent offline reinforcement learning, yet scaling to many-agent systems remains intractable due to the curse of dimensionality in the joint trajectory space. We introduce MF-Diffuser, a framework that lifts trajectory planning to the Wasserstein space of trajectory distributions, where the propagation of chaos ensures a small representative subset of agents captures the full population dynamics. Our approach features a value-weighted chaotic entropy objective that reconciles generative fidelity with return maximization, and a hierarchical coarse-to-fine strategy that progressively grows the agent population during denoising. We establish end-to-end suboptimality bounds with four interpretable terms, revealing that mean-field approximation error scales as $O(H^2/\sqrt{N})$ while offline distribution shift provably does not grow with population size $N$, and prove the generated policy is an approximate mean-field Nash equilibrium with explicit convergence guarantees. Experiments on three mean-field RL benchmarks -- spanning stage games, sequential dynamics, and adversarial team competition -- show MF-Diffuser achieves the best return in the majority of settings, with the largest gains on suboptimal offline data and at extreme scales ($N \geq 10^3$).

infographic.key_insight: MF-Diffuser makes offline multi-agent diffusion planning scalable by modeling many-agent behavior in mean-field trajectory-distribution space instead of the full joint trajectory space.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables offline training and deployment of large-scale coordination policies for systems with thousands of agents while retaining theoretical guarantees on approximation error and equilibrium quality.
method: Lift trajectory planning to Wasserstein space over trajectory distributions.
Use a value-weighted chaotic entropy objective to balance return maximization and generative fidelity.
Apply a hierarchical coarse-to-fine denoising scheme that gradually expands the agent population.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three mean-field RL benchmarks covering stage games, sequential dynamics, and adversarial team competition, the method achieves the best return in most settings, especially with suboptimal offline data and at scales of N >= 10^3.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality of the mean-field approximation and offline data coverage, so systems with weak representative-agent structure or severe distribution mismatch may be harder to scale reliably.
infographic.paper_title: Mean-Field Diffuser: Scaling Offline MARL to Thousands of Agents

title: Neural Operator-Based Surrogate Model for CFD:Helical Coil Steam Generator in Small Modular Reactor
authors: Minseo Lee, Seongmin Oh, Chaehyeon Song, Bumjin Cho, Shilaj Baral, Sangam Khanal
abstract: Real-time thermal-hydraulic simulation is essential for digital twin (DT) technology that supports the safe and efficient operation of small modular reactors (SMRs). Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) provides high-fidelity flow analysis, but its computational cost prevents direct use in DT applications. AI-based surrogate modeling has been actively investigated to address this limitation, yet neural operator--based surrogates for CFD-level transient analysis of SMR-specific geometries have not been reported. This study presents an integrated framework that combines a reduced-order model (ROM) with neural operators, applied to the helical coil steam generator (HCSG) of the System-integrated Modular Advanced Reactor (SMART). Two ROM strategies tailored to each CFD data type were compared, an MLP-based autoencoder (AE) for unstructured mesh data and a convolutional autoencoder (CAE) for structured mesh data, and each was coupled with the deep operator network (DeepONet) to construct the latent DeepONet (L-DeepONet). The Fourier neural operator (FNO) was additionally adopted for comparison. A multi-scale technique was incorporated into both frameworks to mitigate spectral bias and improve the prediction of Kármán vortex streets developing inside the HCSG. The multi-scale L-DeepONet captured the instantaneous periodic vortex dynamics in both velocity and pressure fields, while the FNO and its multi-scale variant predicted the time-averaged mean flow and provided reliable pressure drop estimates. These complementary characteristics provide a practical model-selection guideline that links each architecture to specific DT objectives based on CFD data type and the required level of flow resolution.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid reduced-order plus neural-operator framework can accelerate CFD-like thermal-hydraulic prediction for SMR digital twins while preserving key flow dynamics in a helical coil steam generator.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster transient simulation for reactor monitoring and decision support, with model choice guided by whether the target is instantaneous vortex-resolved fields or mean-flow/pressure-drop estimation.
method: ROM + DeepONet on unstructured mesh data using an MLP autoencoder to form L-DeepONet
ROM + DeepONet on structured mesh data using a convolutional autoencoder to form L-DeepONet
Fourier neural operator (FNO) and multi-scale variants for comparison and spectral-bias mitigation
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the multi-scale L-DeepONet captured instantaneous periodic vortex dynamics in velocity and pressure, while FNO variants predicted mean flow and pressure drop reliably.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on CFD data type and target fidelity; operator models may still struggle with fine transient details if training data are limited or the flow regime shifts.
infographic.paper_title: Neural Operator-Based Surrogate Model for CFD:Helical Coil Steam Generator in Small Modular Reactor

title: When Should Models Change Their Minds? Contextual Belief Management in Large Language Models
authors: Haoming Xu, Weihong Xu, Zongrui Li, Mengru Wang, Yunzhi Yao, Chiyu Wu
abstract: Long-horizon interactions require language models to manage accumulating information: when to update their state, when to preserve their state, and what to ignore. We study this challenge as \textbf{Contextual Belief Management (CBM)}: maintaining a predicted belief state aligned with formal evidence while isolating task-irrelevant noise. To make CBM measurable, we introduce BeliefTrack, a closed-world benchmark spanning Rule Discovery and Circuit Diagnosis, where a finite belief space and symbolic verifiers enable exact turn-level evaluation. BeliefTrack diagnoses three failures: Failed Stay, Failed Update, and Failed Isolation. Across multiple LLMs, vanilla models exhibit severe CBM failures, while explicit belief-tracking prompts provide limited gains. In contrast, reinforcement learning with belief-state rewards reduces failure rates by 70.9\% on average. Further probing reveals latent belief-state dynamics behind these failures, and representation-level steering reduces failure rates by 46.1\% across two tasks\footnote{Code is coming soon at https://github.com/zjunlp/CBM.

infographic.key_insight: Large language models need explicit contextual belief management: they should update, retain, or ignore information depending on evidence, and vanilla prompting often fails at this.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For long-horizon AI systems, the results suggest that state management should be designed and trained explicitly, because reinforcement learning and representation steering can substantially improve reliability.
method: Introduced Contextual Belief Management (CBM) as a framework for belief update/retain/ignore decisions.
Built BeliefTrack, a closed-world benchmark with finite belief spaces and symbolic verifiers for exact turn-level scoring.
Compared vanilla LLMs, belief-tracking prompts, reinforcement learning with belief-state rewards, and representation-level steering.
infographic.evidence_signal: BeliefTrack evaluates turn-by-turn performance on two tasks—Rule Discovery and Circuit Diagnosis—and reports that RL with belief-state rewards reduces CBM failure rates by 70.9% on average.
infographic.watch_item: Because the benchmark is closed-world with symbolic verification, gains may not fully transfer to open-ended real-world settings where belief states are ambiguous and evidence is noisier.
infographic.paper_title: When Should Models Change Their Minds? Contextual Belief Management in Large Language Models

title: Modularizing Educational LLM-Agency for Fostering Responsible Learning Assistance
authors: Julius Gabelmann, Felix Jahn, Kevin Baum, Sophie van Rossum, Emely Wuenscher, Timo P. Gros
abstract: The widespread adoption of AI chatbots in education will drastically change learning, making responsible deployment a critical concern. While large language models (LLMs) might have access to sources discussing insights from educational sciences, they are not particularly inclined to adhere to pedagogical concepts, risking negative effects on the learning process, such as a loss of transfer capabilities, critical thinking, or creativity. In this paper, we introduce an agentic AI chatbot architecture assisting students with exercise solving, specifically designed to contribute to more responsible AI use in education. We base our conceptual development on the identification of several desiderata for responsible LLM-based educational systems, argue for the structural shortcomings inherent in monolithic, out-of-the-box solutions, and instead suggest modularizing the agentic architecture. We propose specific modules for different stages of exercise solving, enabling incorporation of targeted pedagogical advice, guiding students through the learning process in a more controllable, transparent, and overseeable manner.

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that educational LLM assistants should be modular and agentic rather than monolithic so they can better support responsible, pedagogically aligned learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For AI education systems, the proposed modular architecture offers a more controllable and transparent way to embed targeted teaching strategies into student-facing exercise-solving tools.
method: Identify desiderata for responsible LLM-based educational systems.
Analyze why out-of-the-box monolithic chatbots are structurally insufficient.
Propose stage-specific modules for exercise-solving that can incorporate pedagogical guidance.
infographic.evidence_signal: This is a conceptual design paper grounded in a literature- and theory-based analysis rather than in reported experiments or benchmark results in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: A modular agentic system may be harder to implement consistently across stages and still requires careful oversight to ensure pedagogical advice is applied correctly.
infographic.paper_title: Modularizing Educational LLM-Agency for Fostering Responsible Learning Assistance

title: On Distributional Reinforcement Learning in Chaotic Dynamical Systems
authors: James Rudd-Jones, Mirco Musolesi, María Pérez-Ortiz
abstract: Chaotic dynamical systems pose a fundamental challenge for Reinforcement Learning (RL): exponential sensitivity to initial conditions induces high-variance bootstrap targets and poorly conditioned gradient updates. Chaotic dynamics arise across scientific and engineering domains, from fluid flows and climate systems to multi-agent systems, where reliable learning is highly desirable. Standard RL methods optimise expected returns through scalar value functions, implicitly averaging over diverging trajectories and entangling trajectory level instability with the learning objective. We show that under mild statistical stability assumptions, the return distribution evolves more regularly than individual trajectories when measured under the $1$-Wasserstein metric, yielding a smoother distributional Bellman objective. By aligning optimisation with this measure level structure, distributional RL provides better conditioned learning. We offer a principled explanation for the advantages of distributional methods in chaotic systems and the geometries of RL objectives under chaos.

infographic.key_insight: In chaotic dynamical systems, distributional reinforcement learning can be better conditioned than standard value-based RL because the return distribution evolves more smoothly than individual trajectories under the 1-Wasserstein metric.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a more stable learning objective for control and optimization problems in science and engineering domains where chaos makes expected-return RL highly unstable.
method: Analyze RL in chaotic systems through the geometry of return distributions rather than scalar value estimates.
Use the 1-Wasserstein distance to show that distributional Bellman updates can remain smoother under chaos.
Provide a principled theoretical explanation for why distributional methods may outperform standard RL when trajectories diverge rapidly.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper is primarily theoretical: the abstract reports a mild statistical stability assumption and a 1-Wasserstein analysis, but does not mention experiments or benchmark data.
infographic.watch_item: The claimed advantage depends on statistical stability assumptions, so practical gains may weaken if the system violates those assumptions or if the Wasserstein-based update is expensive to estimate.
infographic.paper_title: On Distributional Reinforcement Learning in Chaotic Dynamical Systems

title: Double-Edged Sword or Sharp Tool? Designing and Evaluating Triadic LLM-Teacher Collaboration for K-12 Writing at Scale
authors: Canran Wang, Yuwen Yang, Zhen Wang, Ming Ma, Ding Yu, Chentai Wang
abstract: The double-edged sword of integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) requires an effective triadic collaboration mechanism among LLMs, teachers and students, especially for K-12 education. By developing a triadic collaboration system to support K-12 writing learning, a multidimensional evaluation framework grounded in Systemic Functional Linguistics and the suggestion trajectory tracing pipeline, this paper contributes a large-scale empirical dataset involving $57,954$ essays from $10,195$ students across $120$ schools over two years. Our findings confirm the efficacy of this system in improving writing quality through a strategic labor division: the LLM serves as a generative engine to mitigate teacher burnout, and the teacher acts as a pedagogical gatekeeper and bridge to guarantee feedback quality. While both LLM and teacher are critical for skill improvement, we uncover a ceiling effect where excessive linguistic expansion yields diminishing marginal utility. These suggest a dynamically adaptive LLM-teacher collaboration as student proficiency increases.

infographic.key_insight: A triadic LLM-teacher-student workflow can improve K-12 writing by using the LLM for scalable idea generation while the teacher filters, guides, and validates feedback.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The paper offers a deployable collaboration design and evaluation pipeline for building education-grade LLM systems that reduce teacher workload without sacrificing feedback quality.
method: Built a triadic collaboration system for K-12 writing support.
Used a multidimensional evaluation framework grounded in Systemic Functional Linguistics.
Traced suggestion trajectories to study how LLM and teacher feedback affect student revisions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study analyzes 57,954 essays from 10,195 students across 120 schools over two years, providing large-scale empirical evidence for the system.
infographic.watch_item: The reported ceiling effect suggests that more linguistic expansion from the LLM can yield diminishing returns, so adaptation to student proficiency is necessary.
infographic.paper_title: Double-Edged Sword or Sharp Tool? Designing and Evaluating Triadic LLM-Teacher Collaboration for K-12 Writing at Scale
